note: This early review argues ChatGPT can produce human-like prose that threatens traditional assessment, so universities should rethink how they evaluate learning, weighing both opportunities and risks for students, teachers and institutions.
title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
authors: Jürgen Rudolph, Samson Tan, Shannon Tan
abstract: ChatGPT is the world’s most advanced chatbot thus far. Unlike other chatbots, it can create impressive prose within seconds, and it has created much hype and doomsday predictions when it comes to student assessment in higher education and a host of other matters. ChatGPT is a state-of-the-art language model (a variant of OpenAI’s Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) language model) designed to generate text that can be indistinguishable from text written by humans. It can engage in conversation with users in a seemingly natural and intuitive way. In this article, we briefly tell the story of OpenAI, the organisation behind ChatGPT. We highlight the fundamental change from a not-for-profit organisation to a commercial business model. In terms of our methods, we conducted an extensive literature review and experimented with this artificial intelligence (AI) software. Our literature review shows our review to be amongst the first peer-reviewed academic journal articles to explore ChatGPT and its relevance for higher education (especially assessment, learning and teaching). After a description of ChatGPT’s functionality and a summary of its strengths and limitations, we focus on the technology’s implications for higher education and discuss what is the future of learning, teaching and assessment in higher education in the context of AI chatbots such as ChatGPT. We position ChatGPT in the context of current Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd) research, discuss student-facing, teacher-facing and system-facing applications, and analyse opportunities and threats. We conclude the article with recommendations for students, teachers and higher education institutions. Many of them focus on assessment.
explain_beginner: This paper looks at ChatGPT, a chatbot that can write surprisingly human-like text in seconds. The authors reviewed existing research and tried the tool themselves. They found that ChatGPT could make traditional ways of testing students, like essays and exams done at home, much harder to trust. The paper says universities need to rethink how they check what students have learned. It also points out both possible benefits and risks for students, teachers and schools. The main message is that assessment must change because AI writing tools are here to stay.
explain_business: For executives in higher education, this paper signals that AI chatbots like ChatGPT can produce convincing written work, which undermines conventional assessment such as take-home essays. The authors recommend that institutions rethink how they evaluate learning and consider both opportunities and risks for students, teachers and the organisation. The decision this informs is whether to invest in new assessment methods, staff training and policies around AI use. It also highlights OpenAI's shift from non-profit to commercial business, showing that AI tools will keep advancing, so institutions should act rather than wait.
explain_practitioner: The authors conducted an extensive literature review and hands-on experiments with ChatGPT, a variant of OpenAI's GPT language model. They describe its functionality, strengths and limitations, then position it within Artificial Intelligence in Education research. They examine student-facing, teacher-facing and system-facing applications and analyse opportunities and threats. The paper is among the first peer-reviewed journal articles on ChatGPT in higher education. It concludes with recommendations for students, teachers and institutions, many focused on assessment. The key result is that ChatGPT's human-like prose threatens traditional assessment, so evaluation methods need rethinking.
